issue.title: Should AI stand in for one of the two experts who read a breast screen?
issue.question: Should the NHS let an AI take the place of one of the two human experts who read a woman's breast screen, and who should decide?
issue.summary: Recruitment has started at Cambridge, the first of 30 hospitals in EDITH, a trial of AI in NHS breast screening, according to BBC reporting carried by the Copenhagen Post. Today two human experts read each screen. Women in the trial are randomly put into one of three groups: two experts as now, or AI used in one of two ways, either to review after the expert or to rate the risk before the experts read. The trial's information says "All images will be looked at by at least one human expert", and a woman can decline AI and have two experts read her images without it. Government support is £11 million, and the trial is expected to run about three years.

news.headline: AI-assisted NHS breast screening trial begins taking in women, with up to 700,000 to be invited

poll.pollster: Focaldata (for King's Health Partners, Responsible AI UK and the Policy Institute at King's College London)
poll.finding: If an NHS-approved AI system disagreed with a doctor's diagnosis, 55% said a second doctor should review before any decision is made and 7% said they would follow the AI's advice because it may be more accurate. This is not the same question as whether AI should replace one of two screen readers.
